## Overview

### Why this matters

Most results in computational biology come out of a chain of steps: data are
downloaded and cleaned, programs run with particular settings, figures made
from the output. A paper describes that chain in a few paragraphs, and the
details that decide the result (a software version, a parameter, a sample left
out) are rarely among them. When the chain cannot be rerun, nobody can check a
surprising result, find where an error came in, or build on the work without
starting over, and that includes the authors. The evidence below shows that
this is common, and that the causes are mostly ordinary. The first person to
gain from a reproducible analysis is you: when a reviewer asks for one more
figure, or when you come back to the project after a year (Markowetz 2015).

### What you do in this lesson

This page gives the key ideas in one page, then turns them into a skill you
will use all your career: looking at a published study and judging, in half an
hour, whether you could check or reuse its results.

### Learning outcome

After this page you can **audit** a published study's data, code and
computational environment against the five pillars of computational
reproducibility and the FAIR principles, and **point to** the single change
that would help a reader most.

Check: your written audit of one paper, with evidence (links) for every row.

## 1. Key ideas, in one page

- **Words.** *Reproducible*: same data, same analysis, same result.
  *Replicable*: new data, same analysis, consistent result. *Robust*: same data,
  different analysis. *Generalizable*: new data, new analysis (The Turing Way;
  NASEM 2019). Reproducibility is the minimum: if a result cannot be
  reproduced from its own data and code, a failed replication cannot tell you
  whether the biology or the analysis was wrong.
- **Size of the problem.** In a survey of about 1,500 researchers (Baker 2016)
  more than 70% had failed to reproduce someone else's experiment. For
  computational papers in *Science*, code and data could be obtained for 44%
  and results reproduced for 26% (Stodden et al. 2018). The Reproducibility
  Project: Cancer Biology planned 193 experiments from 53 papers and could
  repeat 50 from 23; the data needed to compute effect sizes was public for 4
  of the 193 (Errington et al. 2021).
- **Causes.** Mostly honest: undocumented steps, manual edits, missing data or
  code, software that changed, incentives that reward novelty over care. Fraud
  exists but is rare.
- **What's in it for you** (Markowetz 2015): working reproducibly helps you
  avoid disasters (an error found before publication, not after), makes
  papers easier to write and reviewers easier to answer, lets your work go on
  in the lab after you leave, and builds your reputation.
- **The five pillars** (Ziemann et al. 2023), each an answer to one of those
  causes:
  - *literate programming*: code, results and explanation in one document,
    so no step goes unrecorded;
  - *code version control and sharing*: every change is recorded, and the
    code a reader needs is public;
  - *compute environment control*: the same software versions, rebuilt on
    any computer;
  - *persistent data sharing*: data deposited with an identifier, so it can
    still be found years later;
  - *documentation*: what to run, in which order, and why.
- **Open science**: open access, open data (FAIR), open code, open methods. It
  helps others check and reuse your work and helps you (shared data is cited
  more: Piwowar et al. 2007). FAIR is not the same as open: sensitive data can
  be FAIR under controlled access.

## 2. The audit rubric

Auditing other people's work is the fastest way to learn what your own will
need: every "missing" you write down is something a reader of *your* paper
would also miss.

For each row, look for evidence in the paper (data and code availability
statements, methods, supplement) and in what it links to. Score each row:
**missing**, **decent**, **good** or **great**. The decent, good and great
levels for data, code and environment follow the NBIS course.

| Row | Decent | Good | Great |
|-----|--------|------|-------|
| **Data** | available on request; metadata needed for the results available | raw data in a public repository; preprocessing done by scripts, not by hand | a section or repository that helps reproduction; open, machine-readable formats (CSV, not XLS) |
| **Code** | code from processed data available on request | all code from raw data public, with versions (tags, releases) | documented, with instructions to reproduce; seeds recorded for random methods |
| **Environment** | key programs named in the methods | all programs **with versions** listed | instructions or files that rebuild the whole environment (lock file, container) |
| **FAIR** | findable: a persistent identifier (DOI, accession) | accessible over a standard protocol, interoperable formats | reusable: license, provenance, rich metadata |
| **License** | some license somewhere | licenses for data and code stated | appropriate licenses (e.g. CC0/CC BY data, MIT/BSD/GPL code) |
| **Documentation** | a README exists | the README says how to run things, in which order | one command or a workflow reproduces the results, and someone has checked |

## 3. Worked example: SARS-CoV-2 in Scotland's wastewater

The same dataset you will judge against FAIR, letter by letter, in
[lesson 03](03-data-management.qmd):

- Paper: Scorza LCT, Cameron GJ, Murray-Williams R, Findlay D, et al. (2022).
  SARS-CoV-2 RNA levels in Scotland's wastewater. *Scientific Data* 9:713.
  <https://doi.org/10.1038/s41597-022-01788-3>
- Data: Zenodo, <https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.6339631> (CC BY 4.0)
- Code: GitHub, <https://github.com/BioRDM/COVID-Wastewater-Scotland>

What we found (checked 2026-10-24):

| Row | Score | Evidence |
|-----|-------|----------|
| Data | **great** | Curated data on Zenodo with a DOI, as CSV; the curation from the original agency data is done by scripts (`src/data_transformations/`) |
| Code | **good to great** | All curation and figure code public on GitHub, with tagged releases (`RC-1.2.0` to `RC-1.2.2`); the README lists the order in which to run the scripts |
| Environment | **decent** | `Installation.R` installs the R packages (`sgo`, `tidyr`, `lubridate`, `tidyverse`) but pins no versions, and the R version is not given. Rerun in five years, the packages will be different |
| FAIR | **great** | DOI with versions (V1.2), CSV, README, linked paper and code |
| License | **good** | CC BY 4.0 for the data, and the repository's `LICENCE` is also CC BY 4.0; a software license (MIT, BSD) would be the usual choice for the code |
| Documentation | **good** | README per folder; `CITATION.cff`, `.zenodo.json` and a `CHANGELOG.md` in the repository |

**The one change that would help most:** record the environment: the R
version and package versions, ideally in a lock file (for R, for example with
`renv`, or with Pixi from conda-forge). Everything else is unusually good:
this is a model to learn from, not a bad example.

## 4. Your turn

1. Pick a paper: one you cite in your own work, or one from the reading list.
   A recent paper in a journal with a data and code policy makes a fair test.
2. Copy the template below into a file (for example `docs/audit.md` in your
   capstone project, once you create it in lesson 02).
3. Fill in every row, with **a link or quotation as evidence**. "Data
   available on request" counts as decent at best.
4. Write the single change that would help a reader most.
5. Optional: try to get one number from the paper's data or code. How long did
   it take? What stopped you?

```{.markdown filename="audit.md" .write}
# Reproducibility audit

Paper: <!-- authors, year, title, journal, DOI -->
Audited by: <!-- name --> on <!-- date -->

| Row | Score (missing / decent / good / great) | Evidence (links, quotes) |
|-----|------------------------------------------|--------------------------|
| Data | | |
| Code | | |
| Environment | | |
| FAIR | | |
| License | | |
| Documentation | | |

The one change that would help most:

Could I reproduce one number? How long did it take, and what stopped me?
```

## Break it: a link that changes under you

A DOI should point to *one thing*. Zenodo gives two kinds: a **concept DOI**
for "the latest version" and a **version DOI** for one exact version. The
Scotland dataset's concept DOI is `10.5281/zenodo.6339631`. Ask Zenodo what it
resolves to today:

```{.bash .run}
pixi exec python -c "
import json, urllib.request
r = json.load(urllib.request.urlopen('https://zenodo.org/api/records/6339631'))
print('concept DOI:', r['conceptdoi'])
print('resolves to:', r['doi'], '- version', r['metadata']['version'], '- published', r['metadata']['publication_date'])
"
```

```text
concept DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.6339631
resolves to: 10.5281/zenodo.6349579 - version V1.2 - published 2022-03-12
```

If a paper cites the concept DOI and the authors publish V1.3 next year, the
same link silently gives readers different data. For a result, cite the
**version** DOI (and record checksums, as you will in lesson 03).

## Apply it to your own project

Before lesson 02, where your capstone starts, audit one paper close to the
analysis you plan for it. What did its authors share that you could build on, and what will
you share better? Keep the audit: it becomes part of your project's README.

## Key points

- Reproducible (same data, same analysis) is the minimum; replicable, robust and generalizable go further.
- Most irreproducibility is honest: missing data, code, environment or documentation.
- Audit data, code and environment separately; the environment is the row most often missing.
- Cite exact versions: version DOIs, tags, lock files.
